facts.statement: Samrukia is known only from a single lower jaw fossil found in Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: Samrukia is a genus of large Cretaceous pterosaurs known only from a single lower jaw discovered in Kazakhstan.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Samrukia was collected from the Santonian-Campanian age Bostobynskaya Formation in the Kyzylorda District.
facts.quote: The holotype and only known specimen was collected from the Santonian-Campanian age Bostobynskaya Formation in Kyzylorda District.

facts.statement: Samrukia was described by Darren Naish, Gareth Dyke, Andrea Cau, François Escuillié, and Pascal Godefroit in 2012.
facts.quote: It was described by Darren Naish, Gareth Dyke, Andrea Cau, François Escuillié, and Pascal Godefroit in 2012

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is named Samrukia nessovi.
facts.quote: The type species is named Samrukia nessovi.

facts.statement: The species name honors paleontologist Lev Nessov, while the genus name refers to Samruk, a magical bird from Kazakh folklore.
facts.quote: The species is named after Lev Nessov, a paleontologist, and the genus is named after Samruk, a magical bird of Kazakh folklore.

facts.statement: Researchers initially interpreted Samrukia as a very large bird with a jawbone twice as long as that of an ostrich.
facts.quote: They interpreted Samrukia as a very large bird (the jawbone is twice as long as that of an ostrich)

facts.statement: If Samrukia could fly, it would have had a wingspan of roughly 4 meters; if it could not fly, it would have stood around 2 to 3 meters tall.
facts.quote: but noted that it is not known whether Samrukia would have been able to fly (in which case they would have had wingspans of roughly 4 m) or not (in which case they would have been around 2 – 3 m tall).

facts.statement: Eric Buffetaut challenged the interpretation of Samrukia as a bird in a 2011 analysis.
facts.quote: A subsequent analysis published by Eric Buffetaut in 2011 challenged the interpretation of Samrukia nessovi as a bird.

facts.statement: Buffetaut argued that characteristics previously identified as avian were actually well known among pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Buffetaut challenged the identification of certain "avian" characteristics identified by Naish et al., claiming that none were definitely avian and that many were in fact well known among pterosaurs.

facts.statement: Buffetaut criticized the original analysis for excluding pterosaurs, noting that the analysis only included birds and other theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: He also criticized the earlier cladistic analysis for not including pterosaurs, but only birds and other theropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Buffetaut concluded that the species was clearly a large pterosaur rather than a giant bird.
facts.quote: Buffetaut stated that the species is "clearly a large pterosaur, not a giant bird."

facts.statement: Darren Naish, one of the original researchers, agreed with Buffetaut's reassessment that Samrukia was a pterosaur.
facts.quote: One of the original researchers who described Samrukia, Darren Naish, agreed with Buffetaut's re-assessment.

facts.statement: Darren Naish admitted that working with fragmentary material was dangerous and realized shortly after publication that Samrukia was a pterosaur, not a bird.
facts.quote: Naish wrote on his Scientific American Web log Tetrapod Zoology: "Working on fragmentary material is dangerous since you can often get things very, very wrong, and I realised within a few days of the paper appearing that Samrukia was no bird. It seemed, in fact, to be a pterosaur."

facts.statement: A review by Averianov et al. suggested Samrukia was an Azhdarchid pterosaur and possibly a synonym of Aralazhdarcho.
facts.quote: A subsequent review by Averianov et al. agreed with the reidentification of the specimen as a pterosaur, and suggested it was an Azhdarchid, possibly a synonym of Aralazhdarcho, which is known from the same formation.

facts.statement: Researchers interpreted Samrukia as a large bird with a mandible twice as long as that of an ostrich.
facts.quote: Ellos interpretaron a Samrukia como una ave de gran tamaño (el hueso mandibular es el doble de largo que el de un avestruz)

facts.statement: If Samrukia could fly, it might have had a wingspan of nearly 4 meters and weighed 12 kg; if it could not fly, it would have been 2 to 3 meters tall and weighed over 50 kg.
facts.quote: pero comentaron que sin otros restos no se sabe si Samrukia era capaz de volar (que si fuera el caso, podría atribuírsele una envergadura alar de cerca de 4 metros, con peso de 12 kg.) o no (en cuyo caso sería un ave de entre 2 – 3 metros de altura, con un peso de más de 50 kg.).

facts.statement: Samrukia lived during the Santonian to Campanian stages, from 85.7 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Campanian (85.7 to 72.2 million years ago)

rejected.statement: An initial analysis classified Samrukia nessovi as a basal member of the bird lineage Ornithuromorpha.
rejected.quote: An initial cladistic analysis by Naish et al. found Samrukia nessovi instead to be a basal member of the bird lineage Ornithuromorpha.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'a basal member of the bird lineage Ornithuromorpha'
